title: Contrast connectors: weighing the populist legacy

sections.content: You know *sin embargo* and *no obstante* from B1 Unit 1: they open a sentence that goes against the one before. You also know *aunque* from A2 Unit 28 (concessive clauses). Historians use them to weigh a legacy, because every government of this period has results that people praise and results that people criticise.

items.spanish: Los gobiernos ampliaron los derechos de los trabajadores. Sin embargo, concentraron mucho poder.
items.english: The governments extended the rights of the workers. However, they concentrated a lot of power.

items.spanish: La industria creció mucho. No obstante, no resolvió todos los problemas del país.
items.english: Industry grew a lot. Nevertheless, it did not solve all the problems of the country.

items.spanish: Aunque cada país era diferente, los trabajadores tuvieron más peso en los tres casos.
items.english: Although each country was different, the workers had more weight in all three cases.

items.spanish: Los seguidores apoyaban al líder; sin embargo, los críticos hablaban de un peligro.
items.english: The followers supported the leader; however, the critics spoke of a danger.

sections.content: *Sin embargo* and *no obstante* start a new sentence (or follow a semicolon) and are followed by a comma. *Aunque* joins two ideas in one sentence and, for a fact, takes the indicative.
